The initial egg of Heteronympha merope is deposited singly on a blade of the host grass, and upon hatching the neonate larva emerges with a wet weight of 0.409 mg [Wwb = 0.409 mg]. The first instar caterpillar, which immediately begins exogenous feeding, possesses a head capsule measuring 0.051 cm  in width, a dimension that increases markedly with each successive moult. During this earliest developmental interval under controlled conditions at a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the larva completes the first stadium in 17.12 days , and the second instar, whose head capsule width reaches 0.086 cm , finishes after 17.4 days .

As the caterpillar progresses through its third and fourth stadia, the allometric expansion of the cranium becomes more pronounced, with the head capsule of the third instar measuring 0.137 cm  and that of the fourth instar attaining 0.22 cm . These intervals are completed in 26.5 days  and 30.9 days , respectively, under the standard thermal conditions of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The progressively longer stadia reflect the increasing energetic demands of a growing larva that must accumulate sufficient reserves for the non-feeding pupal stage. By the time the larva enters its fifth and final instar, the head capsule has reached a width of 0.35 cm ; this terminal feeding stage is the most protracted, lasting 70.3 days  at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C].

Upon completion of the fifth stadium, the larva ceases feeding and undergoes pupation, marking the transition to the quiescent chrysalis. The total time elapsed from birth to the formation of the pupa—the cumulative sum of all five larval stadia—amounts to 162.2 days  when development proceeds at a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The pupa itself represents a metabolically active but non-feeding holometabolic resting stage; its wet weight is 356.6 mg , a substantial increase from the neonatal mass as a consequence of the larval feeding phase. Following the completion of metamorphic reorganisation, the pharate adult undergoes pupal eclosion and then emerges as a fully formed imago after an additional interval of 41.58 days  since the onset of the pupal stage at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C].

The newly eclosed imago has a wet weight of 171.2 mg , notably lighter than the pupa, as mass is lost during the histolysis and histogenesis of metamorphosis and through the expenditure of energy reserves used for wing expansion and cuticle sclerotisation. Once the teneral adult has hardened its exoskeleton, it enters the reproductive phase of its life cycle. The imaginal lifespan, measured from adult eclosion to natural death, extends to 135 days [am = 135 days] when the butterflies are maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a longevity that is comparatively long for a butterfly of this body size. This extended adult stage allows for repeated mating opportunities and the gradual maturation of oocytes over the summer and autumn months in its native southeastern Australian habitat.

Females lay their eggs singly, producing approximately 80 eggs over the entire lifetime , with a typical clutch size of 1 or 2 eggs per oviposition event [N_R_i = 1 or 2 eggs per oviposition event] and a spawning frequency of roughly once every 2.5 days during the peak reproductive period [F_R_i = spawning frequency of roughly once every 2.5 days during the peak reproductive period]. The choice of oviposition site is critical, as the neonate larva must locate suitable host grasses; the survival of the first instar depends heavily on the maternal selection of a microhabitat with adequate thermal buffering and moisture. The species exhibits a single, protracted generation per year in cooler upland regions, though in warmer lowland sites a partial second brood may occasionally be observed, underscoring the strong influence of temperature on the pace of life history in this satyrine butterfly.
